name: Icelandic rímur (epic-chant)
lineage: Icelandic rímur (singular ríma) epic-chant narrative tradition of Iceland, comprising sung-narrative cycles based on Old Norse sagas, Continental medieval romance, and biblical-and-classical sources. Origin documented from late fourteenth-century onward, with continuous transmission through Icelandic farmstead winter-evening-entertainment context (the kvöldvaka evening-vigil reading-and-singing gathering) into the twentieth century. Performance: solo unaccompanied chanting in characteristic narrow-range Phrygian-and-related modes, with the canonical poetic-meter ferskeytt four-line stanza form and elaborate alliterative-and-internal-rhyme conventions inherited from skaldic verse. The Iðunn society (founded 1929) and the Kvæðamannafélagið Iðunn (Iðunn Rímur-singer Society) anchor institutional preservation; the post-2000s neo-folk revival has reactivated the genre.
